title: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration Over Webhook
shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration Over Webhook
summary: Exfiltration Over Webhook abuses the outbound webhook feature of software as a service (SaaS) platforms to push data out of the tenant. A webhook is a URL that a service calls automatically when something changes, so an adversary who can create or edit a webhook in a victim tenant points it at an endpoint they control and lets the platform deliver the content. Two patterns appear: a persistent link that forwards every new message, ticket or email as it arrives, producing continuous automated exfiltration, and one-off manual posts of staged data to a webhook address. Discord, Slack, Teams and generic collectors such as webhook.site are common destinations, and delivery is HTTPS to a mainstream domain. Artefacts include audit log entries for webhook creation, modification or deletion, new integrations and OAuth grants, outbound requests to webhook endpoints from the tenant's egress range, and repeated regular POST requests of similar size. Defenders compare the webhook inventory against approved integrations and alert on endpoints outside corporate or vendor domains.

beginner.definition: Exfiltration over a web service means sending stolen data out through a normal internet service. This version uses a webhook, which is a web address that a service calls by itself when something happens. The attacker adds their own webhook address to a service that you use. From then on, that service sends data out without anyone asking again.
beginner.whyItMatters: Webhooks exist to send data outside your systems, so the traffic is expected and rarely blocked. Once an attacker adds one, data leaves continuously with no user action at all. It can carry emails, chat messages and ticket contents, which often hold sensitive detail. Because the destination may be a well known collaboration service, network tools see nothing unusual.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access to an administrative account in a cloud service such as chat, email or ticketing.
They create a new webhook or integration and set its destination address to a server they control.
The service then posts a copy of each new item to that address, usually over encrypted HTTPS.
Alternatively, the attacker batches stolen data and sends it manually to a webhook address in one request.
Because the destination is often a popular collaboration site, the connection looks like normal business traffic.
Detection comes from audit logs of integration changes and from reviewing where webhooks actually point.
beginner.example: Imagine that you move house and fill in a mail redirection form at the post office. From that day, every letter sent to your old home is quietly delivered to your new address. The post office is only following your written instruction, and nothing about it looks stolen. A webhook works in the same way: the attacker leaves a forwarding address, and the service keeps sending.
takeaways: Every webhook is an outbound path, so keep a list of approved ones and review it often.
Changes to integrations and webhook settings belong in your audit alerts, not only in project notes.
Data can leave continuously without any user action once a webhook is in place.

objectives: Explain what a webhook is and how a service uses it to send data automatically.
Describe the difference between automated webhook exfiltration and manual posting of staged data.
Identify the audit log entries that reveal webhook and integration changes.
Explain why webhook traffic blends into normal cloud service usage.
Describe how to review webhook destinations so that unknown endpoints are found.
